label: Sea-urchin shell outlines match liquid drops flattened by gravity
claim: The vertical outlines of regular sea-urchin shells are the forms of liquid drops depressed by gravity (with the pull of the tube-feet), their degree of flattening varying with the tension or strength of the shell: strong shells (Palaeechinus) stay nearly spherical, soft flexible ones (Phormosoma) are most flattened.
quote: but we have no difficulty in seeing that the various forms represented in a series of sea-urchin shells are no other than those which we may easily and perfectly imitate in drops.
scope: tests of regular echinoids

label: Vessel wall thickness tracks radius in large arteries but falls off in small ones
claim: Under constant pressure the wall thickness of a blood-vessel should vary as its radius (P = T/R); because pressure falls with friction from large to small arteries, wall thickness is proportional to vessel size in larger vessels but becomes disproportionately thin in small arteries and capillaries.
quote: and accordingly we find that while, for a time, the cross-sections of the larger and smaller vessels are symmetrical figures, with the wall-thickness proportional to the size of the tube, this proportion is gradually lost, and the walls of the small arteries, and still more of the capillaries, become exceedingly thin, and more so than in strict proportion to the narrowing of the tube.
scope: arteries and capillaries of vertebrates

label: Heart wall thickness varies inversely with the mean curvature of the chamber
claim: Within each cavity of the heart, where pressure is uniform, wall thickness t varies inversely as the mean curvature, t(1/r + 1/r′) = C, so the highly curved apex of the left ventricle is thinnest.
quote: that is to say, that the thickness (_t_) of the wall varies inversely as the mean curvature.
scope: heart chambers of mammals

label: Left ventricle wall is 6–7 times right's, matching the pressure ratio
claim: The left ventricle requires six to seven times the dilating pressure of the right, and its wall thickness is greater in the same proportion.
quote: we find (1) that we have had to use a pressure in the left ventricle from six to seven times as great as in the right ventricle, and (2) that the thickness of the walls is just in the same proportion.
scope: mammalian hearts

label: Blood-vessels are arranged for minimum effort and minimum wall-surface
claim: The form and arrangement of blood-vessels are such that circulation proceeds with a minimum of effort and a minimum of wall-surface (and hence of friction).
quote: The general principle is that the form and arrangement of the blood-vessels is such that the circulation proceeds with a minimum of effort, and with a minimum of wall-surface, the latter condition leading to a minimum of friction and being therefore included in the first.
scope: vertebrate vascular systems

label: Small arterial branches leave at large angles, large branches at small angles
claim: Small arterial branches come off the main stem at large angles (about 70°–90° for the smallest) and large branches at small angles, with equal branches diverging at equal angles, as Roux's rules state.
quote: In other words, it would seem that for small branches a large angle of bifurcation, and for large branches a small one, is always the better.
scope: arterial branching in vertebrates

label: Optimal branching angle has cosine equal to ratio of energy loss in trunk and branch
claim: The most favourable angle at which an arterial branch leaves its trunk is that whose cosine equals the ratio of energy loss per unit length in the main vessel to that in the branch (cos x = L/L′).
quote: That is to say, the most favourable angle of branching will be such that the cosine of the angle is equal to the ratio of the loss of energy which the blood undergoes, per unit of length, in the main vessel, as compared with that which it undergoes in the branch.
scope: arterial branching in vertebrates

label: Mechanical adaptations of form are demonstrable, unlike colour adaptations
claim: Unlike explanations of colouration as cryptic, warning or mimetic, which cannot be demonstrated, the fitness of organic form for mechanical functions such as swimming or flight can be analysed and established in detail by statics and dynamics.
quote: But of a very different order from all such “adaptations” as these, are those very perfect adaptations of form which, for instance, fit a fish for swimming or a bird for flight. Here we are far above the region of mere hypothesis, for we have to deal with questions of mechanical efficiency where statical and dynamical considerations can be applied and established in detail.
scope: adaptive form and colouration of animals in general

label: Bone is nearly as strong in tension as in compression
claim: Fresh bone resists tearing almost as well as it resists crushing (tensile strength about 9–12 and crushing strength about 13–16 kg per sq. mm), which makes it an economical structural material that can serve equally as tie or strut.
quote: At first sight, bone seems weak indeed; but it has the great and unusual advantage that it is very nearly as good for a tie as for a strut, nearly as strong to withstand rupture, or tearing asunder, as to resist crushing.
scope: fresh (living) vertebrate bone

label: Structures that must resist bending are built as hollow tubes
claim: Where stiffness against bending in all directions is required, organisms use a hollow cylindrical construction with little or no material in the core, as in the thin-walled, almost empty wing bones of long-winged birds such as the albatross, quills, and hollow stems of reeds and straw.
quote: it is appropriate in every case where _stiffness_ is required, where bending has to be resisted. The long bone of a bird’s wing has little or no weight to carry, but it has to withstand powerful bending moments; and in the arm-bone of a long-winged bird, such as an albatross, we see the tubular construction manifested in its perfection
section: Tubular construction of bones and stems
scope: long bones of vertebrates (especially bird wing bones), feather quills and cylindrical plant stems

label: Femoral wall thickness follows the bending-moment distribution along the shaft
claim: Because bending strain is greatest at mid-length of a bent column, the walls of a long bone such as the femur are thickest in the middle of the shaft and thin gradually towards the ends, so that wall thickness forms a graph of the bending moments along the bone.
quote: Hence, if our cylindrical column be exposed to strong bending stresses, it will be prudent and economical to make its walls thickest in the middle and thinning off gradually towards the ends; and if we look at a longitudinal section of a thigh-bone, we shall see that this is just what nature has done.
section: Tubular construction of bones and stems
scope: weight-bearing long bones, especially the human femur

label: Trabeculae of cancellous bone follow the lines of compressive and tensile stress
claim: The trabeculae of cancellous bone, as in the head of the femur, are arranged along the principal lines of compressive and tensile stress of the loaded bone, crossing one another at right angles, exactly as in the engineer's stress diagram of a comparable structure such as a crane-head.
quote: and we have no difficulty in seeing that the anatomical arrangement of the trabeculae follows precisely the mechanical distribution of compressive and tensile stress or, in other words, accords perfectly with the theoretical stress-diagram of the crane.
scope: cancellous bone of weight-bearing vertebrate bones (femur, tibia, calcaneus)

label: Shear removes obliquely laid trabeculae, leaving those aligned with stress lines
claim: Trabecular alignment arises because a trabecula laid down along a pressure or tension line is undisturbed, since there is no shear along those lines, whereas one lying obliquely is acted on by shearing force and displaced until it comes into line with the stress.
quote: If it lie in the direction of one of the pressure-lines, for instance, it will be in a position of comparative equilibrium, or minimal disturbance; but if it be inclined obliquely to the pressure-lines, the shearing force will at once tend to act upon it and move it away.
scope: formation of trabecular bone (and by extension fibre alignment in plants)

label: Trabecular architecture remodels to new force patterns after malunited fracture
claim: Trabecular arrangement is produced by the forces acting on the bone, not by heredity: when a fracture heals with the parts displaced so that the stress lines are redistributed, the trabecular system is entirely remodelled within weeks to align with the new forces, even at a distance from the injury.
quote: If a bone be broken and so repaired that its parts lie somewhat out of their former place, so that the pressure-and tension-lines have now a new distribution, before many weeks are over the trabecular system will be found to have been entirely remodelled, so as to fall into line with the new system of forces.
scope: living vertebrate bone after fracture, malunion or transplantation

label: Mechanical strain directly stimulates growth
claim: A state of strain produced by stress is a direct stimulus to growth, so that tissues under increased load grow stronger or thicker, as when the fibula of a puppy whose tibia was excised grew as thick as or thicker than the normal tibia.
quote: a condition of _strain_, the result of a _stress_, is a direct stimulus to growth itself. This indeed is no less than one of the cardinal facts of theoretical biology.
section: Strain as a stimulus to growth
scope: living tissues of animals and plants, especially bone, skin and supporting plant tissues

label: The quadruped backbone is a double-armed cantilever girder, not an arch
claim: Because the jointed legs cannot resist the horizontal thrust of an arch and there is no tie between its ends, the backbone of a standing quadruped is not an arch, tied arch or bowstring girder but is mechanically comparable to the main girder of a double-armed cantilever bridge.
quote: The structure is not an arch, nor a tied arch, nor a bowstring girder: but it is strictly and beautifully comparable to the main girder of a double-armed cantilever bridge.
scope: vertebral column and associated ligaments of standing quadrupeds

label: Height of vertebral spines is proportional to the local bending moment
claim: In the vertebral girder, ligaments form the upper tension member, vertebral bodies the lower compression member and the spines the web, and the height of the vertebral spines at each point along the back is proportional to the bending moment at that point.
quote: secondly we observe that the depth of the web, or distance apart of the principal members,—that is to say the height of the vertebral spines,—must be proportional to the bending-moment at each point along the length of the girder.
scope: vertebral columns of quadrupedal and bipedal vertebrates

label: Quadrupeds carry more of their weight on the fore-legs than on the hind-legs
claim: In large quadrupeds the fore-legs carry considerably more of the body weight than the hind-legs (about 55–58% in horses and elephants and about two-thirds in camels and llamas).
quote: It will be observed that in all these animals the load upon the fore-feet preponderates considerably over that upon the hind, the preponderance being rather greater in the elephant than in the horse, and markedly greater in the camel and the llama than in the other two.
scope: large terrestrial quadrupedal mammals

label: Heavy heads give tall withers spines; heavy tails give tall lumbar-sacral spines
claim: Animals whose head and neck form a large fraction of body weight have large bending moments over the fore-legs and correspondingly tall spines over the withers, whereas animals with light heads and heavy tails (anteaters, Diplodocus) or that are bipedal (kangaroo, Iguanodon) have their tallest spines over the loins and haunches.
quote: Wherever we have a heavily loaded anterior cantilever arm, that is to say whenever the head and neck represent a considerable fraction of the whole weight of the body, we tend to have large bending-moments over the fore-legs, and correspondingly high spines over the vertebrae of the withers.
scope: terrestrial quadrupedal and bipedal vertebrates, living and fossil

label: Aquatic mammals lack the tall withers and haunch spines of land quadrupeds
claim: Because buoyancy neutralises gravity so that there are no piers or cantilevers, all aquatic mammals (whales, seals, sea-cows) have lost the high arched vertebral spines over the withers and haunches, and aquatic birds have a weak, straight pelvis compared with terrestrial birds.
quote: For here the effect of gravity is neutralised; we have neither piers nor cantilevers; and we find accordingly in all aquatic mammals of whatsoever group—whales, seals or sea-cows—that the high arched vertebral spines over the withers, or corresponding structures over the hind-limbs, have both entirely disappeared.
scope: aquatic mammals (cetaceans, pinnipeds, sirenians) and aquatic birds compared with terrestrial relatives

label: Fish vertebral processes are set at about 120° to one another for uniform stiffness
claim: In ordinary fishes such as cod and haddock (and partly in whales), the backbone is stiffened by three series of ligament-connected processes, dorsal and two transverse, arranged at nearly equal angles of 120°, which gives the greatest and most uniform strength possible for such a system.
quote: And here we see (as we see partly also among the whales), that these three series of processes, or struts, tend to be arranged well-nigh at equal angles, of 120°, with one another, giving the greatest and most uniform strength of which such a system is capable.
scope: vertebral columns of round-bodied fishes and cetaceans

label: Backbone girders are shallower than engineers would build because flexibility is needed
claim: The vertebral girder of large animals such as Diplodocus or Stegosaurus is shallower than an engineer's cantilever of comparable load, because a deeper girder would increase rigidity, and an animal's backbone must combine strength with flexibility.
quote: If we adopt a much greater depth (or ratio of depth to length) as in the modern cantilever, we shall greatly increase the _strength_ of the structure; but at the same time we should greatly increase its _rigidity_, and this is precisely what, in the circumstances of the case, it would seem that nature is bound to avoid.
section: Strength versus flexibility of the backbone
scope: vertebral columns of large vertebrates

label: Skeletal form is largely a diagram of mechanical stress
claim: Skeletal form, as produced by growth, is to a very large extent determined by mechanical stress: material is laid down along the lines of stress so as to avoid shear, from the trabeculae within each bone to the arrangement of the bones in the whole skeleton.
quote: Let us not press either argument or hypothesis too far: but be content to see that skeletal form, as brought about by growth, is to a very large extent determined by mechanical considerations, and tends to manifest itself as a diagram, or reflected image, of mechanical stress.
section: Skeletal form as a diagram of stress
scope: vertebrate skeletons, from bone microstructure to whole-skeleton architecture

label: Mechanically shaped single bones are unreliable guides to phylogenetic affinity
claim: Because the form of bones such as the scapula or vertebrae reflects the mechanical stresses of an animal's mode of life, resemblance or difference in a single such bone is no reliable evidence for or against blood-relationship, as in comparing Zeuglodon with whales.
quote: That the Zeuglodon has a scapula like that of a whale is to my mind no necessary argument that he is akin by blood-relationship to a whale: that his dorsal vertebrae are very different from a whale’s is no conclusive argument that such blood-relationship is lacking.
scope: use of skeletal characters in vertebrate phylogenetics, especially in lineages that changed habitat

label: New mechanical forces modify many correlated parts together, not isolated bones
claim: When altered environment and habits introduce new forces, the resulting modifications of form appear not as isolated changes in single parts but as slow, general, graded modifications spread over many correlated parts or the whole body.
quote: And if this be really so, it will further imply that modifications of form will tend to manifest themselves, not so much in small and _isolated_ phenomena, in this part of the fabric or in that, in a scapula for instance or a humerus: but rather in some slow, _general_, and more or less uniform or graded modification, spread over a number of correlated parts
scope: evolutionary change of form in animals, especially skeletons

label: Organic forms depart from mathematical ideals only as inanimate forms do
claim: There is no essential difference between organic and inorganic form: living forms depart from ideal mathematical figures only because secondary forces act alongside the main one, just as no chain hangs as a perfect catenary and no raindrop is a perfect sphere.
quote: There is no such essential difference between these phenomena of organic form and those which are manifested in portions of inanimate matter. No chain hangs in a perfect catenary and no raindrop is a perfect sphere: and this for the simple reason that forces and resistances other than the main one are inevitably at work.
scope: organic form in general

label: Specific differences in form are mainly differences of relative magnitude
claim: The essential differences in form between species of the same group are differences of proportion or relative magnitude (Aristotle's 'excess and defect'), and these are the main cause of specific differences.
quote: It is precisely this difference of relative magnitudes, this Aristotelian “excess and defect” in the case of form, which our co-ordinate method is especially adapted to analyse, and to reveal and demonstrate as the main cause of what (again in the Aristotelian sense) we term “specific” differences.
section: Specific differences as excess and defect
scope: species within the same zoological class or genus

label: Evolution varies the whole body in correlation, not character by character
claim: Because dissimilar related fishes can be referred as wholes to the same figure in different coordinate systems, variation has proceeded on definite and orderly lines under a comprehensive law of growth affecting the whole structure, rather than by independent variation of separate parts as the usual conception of natural selection assumes.
quote: But if, on the other hand, diverse and dissimilar fishes can be referred as a whole to identical functions of very different co-ordinate systems, this fact will of itself constitute a proof that variation has proceeded on definite and orderly lines, that a comprehensive “law of growth” has pervaded the whole structure in its integrity
scope: evolutionary differentiation of related animal species

label: Related organisms differ by simple, symmetrical Cartesian transformations
claim: The forms of related organisms can, as a general rule, be mapped onto one another by a simple and symmetrical deformation of a Cartesian coordinate grid, such as would result from a slight and simple change in the system of forces acting on the growing organism.
quote: We are dealing in this chapter with the forms of related organisms, in order to shew that the differences between them are as a general rule simple and symmetrical, and just such as might have been brought about by a slight and simple change in the system of forces to which the living and growing organism was exposed.
scope: related species within a zoological class (fishes, crustaceans, reptile and mammal skulls, etc.)

label: Shear-deformed fossils are often mistaken for distinct species
claim: Fossils in folded and inclined strata are often symmetrically deformed, usually by simple shear, so that they have been described as distinct species and occasionally even as new genera.
quote: the contained fossils are apt to be so curiously and yet so symmetrically deformed (usually by a simple shear) that they may easily be interpreted as so many distinct and separate “species.”
scope: fossils in tectonically deformed strata

label: Cannon-bones of ox, sheep and giraffe differ by a simple one-axis stretch
claim: The cannon-bones of the ox, sheep and giraffe differ essentially only in relative length and breadth: at equal length, the sheep's bone is about two-thirds and the giraffe's about one-third as broad as the ox's.
quote: In other words, the main (and perhaps the only) difference between the two bones is simply that that of the sheep is elongated, along the vertical axis, as compared with that of the ox in the relation of 3/2.
scope: metapodial (cannon) bones of ruminant ungulates

label: Ratio of radial to tangential growth about a node yields lanceolate, ovate, cordate leaves
claim: Dicotyledon leaf shapes arise from growth radial to and transverse to radii about a node of no growth at the leaf base; increasing the ratio of tangential to radial growth carries the outline successively from lanceolate to ovate to cordate.
quote: If we now alter the ratio between the radial and tangential velocities of growth—in other words, if we increase the angles between corresponding radii—we pass successively through the various configurations which the botanist describes as the lanceolate, the ovate, and finally the cordate leaf.
scope: leaves of dicotyledons (contrasted with basally growing monocot leaves)

label: The lopsided begonia leaf reflects unequal, not asymmetrical, growth
claim: The two halves of a begonia leaf, one ovate and the other cordate, are mathematically similar figures produced by unequal growth on either side of the midrib, so that angles to equal radii on the two sides are in constant proportion.
quote: the so-called unsymmetrical leaf of a begonia, in which one side of the leaf may be merely ovate while the other has a cordate outline, is seen to be really a case of _unequal_, and not truly asymmetrical, growth on either side of the midrib.
scope: asymmetrical leaves of Begonia

label: Organisms grow along stream lines definable by a mathematical transformation
claim: The law of growth implied by representing related forms as orthogonal coordinate transformations is that the organism grows along stream lines definable by a suitable mathematical transformation; departures from orthogonality reflect the organism not being homogeneous and isotropic.
quote: the “law of growth” which our biological analysis by means of orthogonal co-ordinate systems presupposes, or at least foreshadows, is one according to which the organism grows or develops along _stream lines_, which may be defined by a suitable mathematical transformation.
section: Stream lines and law of growth
scope: growth of organisms in general

label: Many organic forms arise from uniform expansive growth limited by local constraints
claim: Many developmental changes of form are produced by local trammels or lines of constraint acting on otherwise uniform and symmetrical expansive growth, as a ligature turns a gourd into two globes or a muscular band makes the stomach a lopsided bubble.
quote: It is clear, I think, that we may account for many ordinary biological processes of development or transformation of form by the existence of trammels or lines of constraint, which limit and determine the action of the expansive forces of growth that would otherwise be uniform and symmetrical.
scope: development of tubular and vesicular organs (gut, stomach, heart, neural tube) and fruits

label: One transformation accounts for the differences between porcupine-fish and sunfish
claim: Deforming the coordinate grid of Diodon (concentric circles and approximately hyperbolic curves) yields the outline of the sunfish Orthagoriscus, so that a single integral transformation accounts for all their apparently separate external differences while leaving the head region nearly unchanged.
quote: And as such it accounts, by one single integral transformation, for all the apparently separate and distinct external differences between the two fishes.
scope: Diodon and Orthagoriscus (Mola), and by extension related fish genera

label: One harmonious deformation accounts for all skull differences among crocodilians
claim: Across most crocodilian genera, the skull contours and even the shapes and sizes of individual bones and vacuities can be derived from one another by a single simple coordinate transformation, so that the skull of Notosuchus can be reconstructed bone for bone from that of Crocodilus.
quote: To all intents and purposes, then, this not very complex system, representing one harmonious “deformation,” accounts for _all_ the differences between the two figures, and is sufficient to enable one at any time to reconstruct a detailed drawing, bone for bone, of the skull of _Notosuchus_ from the model furnished by the common crocodile.
scope: skulls of crocodilians, living and fossil (excluding the oldest forms such as Belodon)

label: Perissodactyls are more closely related to hares and rabbits than to other ungulates
claim: Since the rabbit's skull is derived from that of a primitive rhinoceros by a simple uniform downward flexure, the Perissodactyla are more closely related to the Leporidae than to other ungulates, and the Leporidae more closely to Perissodactyla than to other rodents.
quote: For my part, I would go further; for I think there is strong reason to believe that the Perissodactyles are more closely related to the Leporidae than the former are to the other Ungulates, or than the Leporidae are to the rest of the Rodentia.
scope: phylogenetic relationships of Perissodactyla, Leporidae, other ungulates and rodents

label: Fossil horse skulls match interpolated stages between Hyracotherium and Equus
claim: Skulls interpolated by coordinate transformation between Hyracotherium (Eohippus) and Equus coincide closely with actual fossil skulls of Mesohippus and Protohippus, which therefore lie on the transformation series from Eohippus to the horse.
quote: it will be seen that the actual fossil skull coincides in the most perfect fashion with one of the hypothetical forms or stages which our method shews to be implicitly involved in the transition from _Hyracotherium_ to _Equus_.
scope: skulls of fossil and living Equidae

label: Parahippus is a divergent offshoot, not on the direct line to Equus
claim: Because the skull of Parahippus fits the interpolated transformation series from Eohippus to Equus poorly, Parahippus is not in the direct line of descent but represents a divergent branch of the Equidae.
quote: In short, though some writers have placed _Parahippus_ in the direct line of descent between _Equus_ and _Eohippus_, we see at once that there is no place for it there, and that it must, accordingly, represent a somewhat divergent branch or offshoot of the Equidae.
scope: phylogeny of fossil Equidae

label: Ape and human skull differences form one continuous, roughly logarithmic transformation
claim: The differences between the human skull and the skulls of the chimpanzee and baboon form one continuous integral deformation in which corresponding areas of the grid increase approximately logarithmically downwards and forwards, rather than separate modifications of jaws, braincase and face.
quote: In both dimensions, as we pass from above downwards and from behind forwards, the corresponding areas of the network are seen to increase in a gradual and approximately logarithmic order in the lower as compared with the higher type of skull; and, in short, it becomes at once manifest that the modifications of jaws, braincase, and the regions between are all portions of one continuous and integral process.
scope: skulls of humans and anthropoid primates

label: Human and anthropoid skulls show divergent rather than linear evolutionary change
claim: No continuous transformation series passes through known fossil and living human and anthropoid skulls (Mesopithecus, Pithecanthropus, Neanderthal, modern man), indicating that there is no single straight line of descent and that their variation has been divergent.
quote: The failure is not the fault of our method. It merely indicates that no one straight line of descent, or of consecutive transformation, exists; but on the contrary, that among human and anthropoid types, recent and extinct, we have to do with a complex problem of divergent, rather than of continuous, variation.
scope: fossil and living hominids and anthropoid apes

label: Depth expansion and lateral compression vary inversely, conserving fish volume
claim: In related fishes, expansion in one transverse dimension tends to be compensated by compression in the other, so that volume at a given length changes less than linear dimensions; the plaice is about twice as deep and half as thick as the haddock and has almost the same length-weight coefficient k = W/L^3.
quote: the very fact that the two dimensions tend to vary _inversely_ already assures us that, in the general process of deformation, the _volume_ is less affected than are the _linear dimensions_.
scope: related fish species differing in body depth and width (e.g. haddock and plaice, shark and skate)

label: A mathematical approach is essential to the study of organic form
claim: A mathematical aspect of morphology, largely neglected by morphologists, is interwoven with their problems, complementary to description, and essential to the proper understanding of form.
quote: My task is finished if I have been able to shew that a certain mathematical aspect of morphology, to which as yet the morphologist gives little heed, is interwoven with his problems, complementary to his descriptive task, and helpful, nay essential, to his proper study and comprehension of Form.
scope: morphology as a science

label: Mathematical regularity and usefulness coincide in living forms
claim: What is most beautiful and regular in natural form, as in the bee's cell, is also found to be most useful and excellent.
quote: Moreover the perfection of mathematical beauty is such (as Maclaurin learned of the bee), that whatsoever is most beautiful and regular is also found to be most useful and excellent.
scope: natural forms generally, exemplified by the honeycomb

label: Living and non-living things are bound alike by physical and mathematical law
claim: Living and non-living things alike are governed by the same physical and mathematical laws.
quote: The living and the dead, things animate and inanimate, we dwellers in the world and this world wherein we dwell,—πάντα γα μὰν τὰ γιγνωσκόμενα,—are bound alike by physical and mathematical law.
scope: all living and non-living matter
